name: Tokenization and PCI Scope
intent: Keep card numbers off your own systems: let the payment provider collect them in hosted fields or on its own page, and keep only a token that is useless anywhere else, so fewer of your systems fall under the card industry's security audit.
scenario: An online shop has a checkout page, a web server, an API, a payment service, a database, a log pipeline, backups and an analytics warehouse. Its first version has a card form on its own page that posts to its own server. The team then moves the card form to the provider's hosted fields, and later to a full redirect, and watches how many of the eight systems the card industry's audit rules cover.
problem: A card number is so valuable to a thief that the card industry's security standard (PCI DSS) puts every system that stores, processes or transmits card data, and every system connected to them, under a long list of controls and regular assessment. If the number travels through your web server, your API and your payment service, all of them are in scope, and so is anything the number leaks into by accident: a log line that records a request body, a nightly backup, an analytics copy of the database. Each in-scope system adds audit work, restricted access and risk, and one breach exposes every card ever stored.

howItWorks.title: Know why scope matters
howItWorks.text: The standard applies to the people and systems that handle cardholder data. The more of your systems touch a card number, the more of them must meet the security requirements and be assessed, and the larger the damage if one is breached. The cheapest control is to not have the data: a system that never sees a card number has nothing to leak and, typically, falls outside the audit, unless it can affect the security of the systems or pages that do. The goal of the design is therefore to shrink the number of systems that ever see one.

howItWorks.title: Collect the number on the provider's side
howItWorks.text: There are three common designs. In the first, your page has the card form and posts the number to your server, so every hop is in scope. In the second, your page embeds fields (often iframes) served by the provider, so the number goes from the customer's browser straight to the provider and your servers never see it, though your page still delivers the code around those fields. In the third, the customer is redirected to a page the provider hosts and comes back with a result. Moving from the first design to either of the others takes your servers out of the card data flow, and the audit effort typically shrinks a lot. Provider fields in an iframe and a full redirect are typically treated alike (in PCI DSS terms both can qualify for the shortest self-assessment questionnaire, SAQ A), while fields that your own page's script builds can leave more in scope. In both, the page that embeds the fields or sends the customer away, and the server that delivers it, stay in scope, because tampering with them could send the card number to an attacker. The price of a redirect is control over the look and flow of checkout.

howItWorks.title: Receive and keep a token, not the number
howItWorks.text: When the provider has the card, it returns a token: a random-looking string that stands for the card inside the provider's vault. Your servers use the token to charge the card, save it for later or refund. A vault token (a random value, the usual kind) has no mathematical link to the number, so nobody can compute the number from it, and it can be restricted to one merchant, so a stolen token is of little use elsewhere. The vault is the only place where the number can be looked up.

howItWorks.title: Tokens are not encryption
howItWorks.text: Encrypted card data can be turned back into the number by anyone who holds the key, so the systems that hold both the data and the key typically stay in scope, and a stolen database plus a stolen key is a stolen card list. A token is looked up in a vault run by someone else. Some card networks also issue network tokens, which replace the card number across the payment flow itself, and are tied to a merchant or a device and to the card account, so they keep working when a physical card is replaced.

howItWorks.title: Keep little, log nothing sensitive
howItWorks.text: What your system usually needs is the token, the last 4 digits, the brand and the expiry date, enough to show "Visa ending 1111" and to charge again. The full number and the security code (CVV) are not to be logged, and the security code must not be stored at all once the payment is authorized. The easy leaks are the quiet ones: request bodies in logs, exception reports that attach form data, support screenshots, analytics events and test data copied from production.

pros: Fewer of your systems fall under the audit, so assessment work and the number of controls to maintain shrink a lot
A breach of your database exposes tokens, not usable card numbers
The provider specialises in this: its vault is built and audited for the job
Tokens let you charge, save and refund cards without ever holding the number
cons: Less control over the card form: hosted fields limit styling, and a redirect takes the customer away from your site
A token is tied to one provider, so moving to another means migrating the cards, which needs the provider's cooperation
Your page is still a target: tampered code on a page that embeds payment fields is an attack on the customer
Scope shrinks, it does not vanish: you still have security duties for the part you keep, and the provider's compliance does not cover your own
whenToUse: Almost every business that takes cards online and is not itself a payment provider
Systems that save cards for later charges, subscriptions and one-click checkout
Teams that want to keep the audit simple and the blast radius of a breach small
whenNotToUse: Payment providers, processors and banks, whose business is to handle card data and who meet the full standard themselves
Cases where the form must be fully custom and the team accepts, and can staff, the larger audit
Non-card payment methods (bank transfers, wallets) that do not involve a card number at all
pitfalls: Logging full request bodies or exceptions that include the card form, which quietly puts card numbers in the log pipeline, backups and monitoring tools
Storing the security code (CVV), which must not be kept after authorization
Calling encryption tokenization, and assuming that encrypted card numbers are out of scope while you hold the key
Embedding third-party scripts on the checkout page, any of which can read what the customer types in a page you serve
Copying production data with card details into test environments or analytics
Believing that the provider's certification covers your own systems and page

roles.label: Customer
roles.description: Types the card number into a payment form.

roles.label: Checkout page
roles.description: Your page: it either has the card form or embeds the provider's.

roles.label: Your servers
roles.description: Web server, API, payment service, database, logs and backups.

roles.label: Payment provider
roles.description: Collects the number, runs the vault and returns a token.

roles.label: Attacker
roles.description: Steals a database dump and looks for card numbers in it.

quiz.question: A checkout page embeds the payment provider's hosted card fields. The customer pays. What does the shop's own server receive?
options: The full card number over TLS, because the form posts to the shop.
A token for the card and the last 4 digits, because the number went from the browser to the provider.
The card number encrypted with the shop's key, so it can be decrypted later.
The number without its security code, so that it is safe to store.
quiz.explanation: With hosted fields the number goes from the customer's browser straight to the provider, so the shop's servers get only a token and display details such as the last 4 digits. That is what keeps them out of the heaviest part of the audit.

quiz.question: A team encrypts card numbers with a strong cipher before saving them in its database and says this puts the database out of audit scope. What is the best answer?
options: Correct: encrypted data is never in scope, whatever happens to the key.
Correct, as long as the key is rotated every year.
Wrong, because encrypted numbers must also be hashed with a salt.
Wrong in general: whoever holds the data and can decrypt it typically remains in scope, unlike a vault token.
quiz.explanation: Encryption is reversible with the key, so systems that can reach both the data and the key still handle card numbers. A token has no mathematical link to the number, and the lookup lives in the provider's vault. Hashing is not a fix, since the shop needs to charge the card.

quiz.question: Which set of card data does a shop generally keep after a payment, for charging again and for showing the customer?
options: The token, the last 4 digits, the brand and the expiry date.
The full number in an encrypted column, plus the security code for refunds.
The full number, but masked in logs and restricted to the support team.
The security code and the last 4 digits, which are enough to charge again.
quiz.explanation: The token charges the card, and the last 4 digits, brand and expiry are enough to identify it to the customer. The full number is what pulls systems into scope, and the security code must not be stored after authorization at all.
